title: Pathologist Salary: Hourly Rates, Annual Pay, Casual Loading and Super
description: Understand pathologist salary calculations: hourly to annual, 38-hour week, fortnightly pay, casual loading, super, tax. Award rates from Fair Work Ombudsman and ABS data.
salarySummary: For a pathologist earning an hourly rate under the Medical Practitioners Award, annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 hours × 52 weeks, with superannuation of 12% paid on top.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual pathologist salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. For example, at $80 per hour, annual pay would be $80 × 38 × 52 = $158,080 before tax and super. Super is paid on top at 12% of ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base.

faqs.q: Does casual loading apply to pathologist salaries?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are employed as a casual pathologist under the Medical Practitioners Award, you are entitled to a 25% casual loading on top of the minimum hourly rate. This loading compensates for entitlements like annual leave and sick leave that casuals do not receive. When using our timesheet, check the casual loading box to add 25% to the base rate – do not enter a rate that already includes loading.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates for pathologists?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage (from 1 July 2026: $26.44 per hour) is the legal floor for all employees not covered by an award or agreement. Pathologists are typically covered by the Medical Practitioners Award [MA000031], which sets higher minimum rates based on classification and experience. Always check the relevant award pay guide from the Fair Work Ombudsman for your correct minimum rate.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the pathologist salary landscape

When researching a **pathologist salary** in Australia, it helps to start with the official sources: the Fair Work Ombudsman, the Fair Work Commission, the Australian Bureau of Statistics, and the Australian Taxation Office. These bodies provide the award rates, minimum wages, average earnings, and tax thresholds that underpin any pay calculation. A pathologist – classified under the Medical Practitioners Award [MA000031] – may earn well above the National Minimum Wage, but the same conversion principles apply.

The Fair Work Commission’s Modern Awards Pay Database contains the calculated minimum rates, allowances and penalty rates for each award, updated after the Annual Wage Review. For pathologists, the relevant award is the Medical Practitioners Award, and the Fair Work Ombudsman provides a pay guide that lists minimum hourly rates for each classification level. These are the rates you should use as a baseline – not recruiter surveys – because they are legally enforceable.

## Converting hourly to annual pay

The core formula on this site is simple: **annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**. We assume a standard full-time week of 38 hours, as defined in the National Employment Standards and most modern awards. If you work part-time or irregular hours, adjust the weekly hours accordingly.

For example, if a pathologist’s hourly rate under the award is $80.00, the annual calculation is:

$80.00 × 38 × 52 = **$158,080** before tax and before super.

To find your fortnightly pay, multiply the weekly amount by 2: weekly pay = $80.00 × 38 = $3,040; fortnightly = $6,080. This is useful for budgeting if you are paid every two weeks.

The [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) page explains this in more detail, and our [timesheet](/) lets you enter your base rate and see the annual, monthly, fortnightly and weekly figures instantly.

## The role of casual loading and superannuation

If you work as a casual pathologist, you are entitled to a **25% casual loading** on top of the minimum hourly rate. This loading compensates for the lack of paid leave entitlements. When using our calculator, you should enter the base award rate (without loading) and then check the casual loading box – the tool will add 25% automatically. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading, as that would double-count it.

Superannuation is paid **on top** of your gross earnings. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee rate is **12%** of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For a pathologist earning $158,080, the employer would contribute an additional $18,969.60 in super (12% of $158,080, well under the cap). This super is not deducted from your pay – it is an extra benefit. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page for more.

## Award coverage and minimum rates

Pathologists are medical practitioners and are covered by the **Medical Practitioners Award 2020**. The award sets minimum hourly rates for different classification levels (e.g., intern, registrar, specialist). The Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guide for this award lists the current rates. For example, a Level 1 medical practitioner may have a minimum rate around $35–$40 per hour, while a specialist pathologist would be classified at a higher level with a correspondingly higher rate.

It is important to check the award because the National Minimum Wage ($26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026) is only a floor. Most pathologists earn above the award rate due to experience, qualifications, or enterprise agreements. The [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page has more on the NMW and award system.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) Survey of Employee Earnings and Hours, May 2025 (customised report cited by Jobs and Skills Australia), the median weekly earnings for full-time non-managerial pathologists are not published in the snippet, but the ABS Average Weekly Earnings for all full-time adult ordinary time employees was $2,083.70 per week as of May 2026. Pathologists typically earn above that average due to their specialised skills.

## Tax and take-home pay considerations

Once you have your annual gross figure, you can estimate your take-home pay using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% on excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30% on excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37% on excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: 45% on excess over $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (based on 2025–26 single reduction thresholds, as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of this reference). For a pathologist earning $158,080, the tax would be approximately:

- Tax on first $18,200: $0
- Tax on $18,201–$45,000: 15% of $26,800 = $4,020
- Tax on $45,001–$135,000: 30% of $90,000 = $27,000
- Tax on $135,001–$158,080: 37% of $23,080 = $8,539.60
- Total tax: $39,559.60
- Medicare levy (2% of $158,080): $3,161.60
- Total deductions: $42,721.20
- Estimated take-home: $115,358.80 per year, or about $2,218 per week.

Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool for a more detailed estimate that includes HELP repayments, Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging if applicable.

Remember: this is an estimate. Your actual pay may differ due to unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. Always refer to your pay slip and the relevant award or agreement.

For a quick reference of average earnings across occupations, see our [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page. And if you need to check award classifications, the [pay guides](/blog) section links to the latest Fair Work Ombudsman documents.

## Disclaimer

Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.
